transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-21
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 37 minutes
Attendees: Liam Shaw (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (Catalyst CTO), Jordan Lee (Lead ML Eng), Alex Park (Infra)

Auto-summary (generated): Discussed quickstart path for Redwood hosted API, eligibility for free credits, pilot success criteria, and security needs for possible Dedicated / Private later.

[00:00] Liam Shaw: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, i'm liam from redwood inference, and i'm joined by priya on the se side. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya Torres: good, thanks. uh excited to chat, we've been poking around the docs and wanted to get a sense for how fast we can actually start sending requests — time to first token is the big metric for us.
[00:15] Liam Shaw: totally, that's our sweet spot. for most PLG teams the hosted api gets you to first token in minutes; we'll walk through the exact steps and i'll share credits so you can run a small experiment.
[00:24] Priya Kapoor: just to add, i'll outline a minimal p o c flow so you can validate latency and cost with a couple of sample prompts.
[00:30] Jordan Lee: quick context: we want an embeddings pipeline + a summarization endpoint. expected burst qps is around 30–50, average request size 400 tokens. we also care about p95 latency under 350ms for text generation if possible.
[00:43] Alex Park: and infra-wise we need to know data residency — we have EU customers so we may need private or a region pinned deployment, and of course KMS integration for keys.
[00:55] Liam Shaw: great, that's clear. so three threads: 1) get you to first token quickly via hosted (free credits + quickstart), 2) validate performance and cost, 3) evaluate dedicated or private for residency and KMS.
[01:08] Maya Torres: yep. two quick questions upfront: SOC 2? and sso for the console?
[01:12] Priya Kapoor: redwood has SOC 2 type 2 — i'll attach the audit summary in the security pack. Console supports SAML SSO and team-level RBAC. for private we also support customer-managed KMS/HSM for at-rest and in-flight key wraps.
[01:26] Jordan Lee: when you say "hosted gets you to first token in minutes" — is that assuming we already have an api key and we paste a curl? any SDK required?
[01:33] Liam Shaw: you can do it with curl or our SDKs. the steps are: sign up, redeem trial credits, get api key, run a single request (we have a sample repo). the fastest path is literally copy -> paste -> receive tokens — usually under 5 minutes for an engineer reading the quickstart.
[01:49] Maya Torres: okay, so what's in the free credits — is it per token? per hour?
[01:53] Liam Shaw: trial credits are numeric dollars that apply to your hosted usage; they cover calls, embeddings, and tokens by our normal usage billing. we'll send a redemption link and a quick guide on cost control like max tokens per request and per-minute rate limits.
[02:05] Alex Park: about latency — for p95 350ms we might need dedicated instances close to EU region. can you do region pinning for hosted?
[02:13] Priya Kapoor: hosted has regional endpoints; for strict latency SLOs and predictable throughput, dedicated provides pinned GPU capacity in the region and autoscaling rules. private gives full control but has a longer setup time.
[02:24] Jordan Lee: curious about kv cache behavior — we have long multi-turn chat sessions and want to avoid repeated compute. do you do prefix caching?
[02:30] Priya Kapoor: yes, runtime supports KV cache and prefix/KV caching to cut down per-token compute. i'll note that caching efficiency depends on your prompt shapes; we'll show you how to enable it in the POC. sometimes the transcriber writes it as "K-V cash" in our logs but it's the same thing.
[02:42] Maya Torres: (laughs) noted. on the security front, for private deployments do you support on-prem air-gapped or only VPC?
[02:49] Liam Shaw: we support both: VPC-hosted private control plane and an on-prem package for air-gapped customers. on-prem has additional steps — network ops and a longer lead time, usually measured in weeks not days.
[03:02] Alex Park: timeline — if we decide to pilot, what is realistic time-to-pilot for hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[03:09] Priya Kapoor: hosted: minutes to hours (to first token) and a week to run meaningful load tests. dedicated: provisioning and capacity commitments take a few weeks; private on-prem: typically 4–8 weeks depending on approvals.
[03:24] Jordan Lee: ok good. do you have benchmarks for 50 qps embedding workloads cost numbers?
[03:29] Liam Shaw: we have example cost calculators, and i'll share a spreadsheet with sample workloads mapped to costs for hosted vs dedicated. the optimize toolkit gives batching/quant recommendations that can cut cost by 40–60% for embeddings.
[03:42] Maya Torres: regarding compliance docs, can you send SOC2, ISO certs, data processing addendum?
[03:47] Priya Kapoor: yes, security pack includes SOC2, ISO summaries, DPA, and the KMS integration guide. we'll redact any PII.
[03:55] Liam Shaw: just FYI — if you want to keep tokens/data in your VPC for inference we can do private with customer-managed key and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM.
[04:05] Alex Park: nice, audit forwarding is important. how about model governance — can we pin model versions and do rollbacks?
[04:11] Priya Kapoor: yes, rollout policies include canary, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to a compatible variant. version pinning is supported across hosted/dedicated/private.
[04:20] Jordan Lee: sweet. for the POC can we test both the summarization endpoint and embeddings in the same credit bucket?
[04:25] Liam Shaw: absolutely. credits apply across all hosted usage. one suggestion is to run a small embedding-only pass first to validate cost and then the text gen tests for latency.
[04:34] Maya Torres: would you recommend any quantized model or is hosted using your own optimized variants?
[04:38] Priya Kapoor: hosted has a model catalog; we also host quantized variants where appropriate. for cost-sensitive embedding workloads we suggest 8-bit quant and batching. we'll recommend specific model names in the follow-up.
[04:49] Jordan Lee: any gotchas for AWS vs GCP regions? we run primarily in GCP europe-west1.
[04:55] Priya Kapoor: we have EU regions in both clouds; for private deployments we do VPC peering and routes. some kernels behave slightly differently across GPU types but our runtime hides most differences. we'll list recommended instance types in the POC runbook.
[05:09] Liam Shaw: ok let's talk success criteria — what do you want to measure in a 2-week pilot?
[05:13] Maya Torres: p95 latency under 350ms for gen, embedding cost under $X per 1k, and seamless SSO + audit logs for our security team. also, minimal engineering time to integrate — less than 3 engineer-days.
[05:26] Liam Shaw: good measurable goals. we'll put those in the POC scope doc.
[05:30] Alex Park: i just want to flag procurement — our buying process needs a master services agreement and some custom language around data residency. how long does enterprise contracting usually take?
[05:40] Liam Shaw: for Dedicated/Private customers we've seen 4–8 weeks with legal review; hosted self-serve is faster — usually you can sign up and experiment without contract, then enterprise sales engage when you need committed capacity or custom terms.
[05:53] Jordan Lee: one practical question — do you provide a sandbox repo or postman collection for quickstart?
[05:58] Priya Kapoor: yes, we'll share a github repo with examples in curl, python, js, plus a postman collection. that will be in the quickstart email.
[06:06] Maya Torres: awesome. i have a small worry — we've built an internal transformer infra before and it was a nightmare to maintain. if we go private later, how much ops overhead should we expect?
[06:17] Priya Kapoor: private takes more ops, but our private package includes maintenance tooling, upgrade scripts, and optional managed support. we'd align on an ops model in the SLA.
[06:27] Liam Shaw: okay, i want to recap so we've got alignment on next steps — liam to send quickstart + credits, priya to send POC runbook and recommended model/config, maya to share dataset + qps expectations, and we schedule a 60-min POC next week. does that sound right?
[06:42] Maya Torres: yes. can we do the POC 2027-04-28?
[06:46] Liam Shaw: that works for us — i'll propose time and loop in priya.
[06:49] Jordan Lee: one last small nit — do you have a way to cap spending on the credits so we don't blow through them accidentally?
[06:56] Priya Kapoor: yes, the console supports usage quotas and token limits per api key; we'll show the recommended guardrails in the quickstart.
[07:04] Alex Park: perfect.
[07:06] Liam Shaw: all right thanks everyone — we'll get those artifacts over. looking forward to it.
[07:10] Maya Torres: thanks, talk soon.
[07:12] (call ends)

Post-call notes:
- Maya mentioned potential procurement concerns and custom DPA; loop in legal early if pilot shows promise.
- Priya to prepare minimal benchmark scripts (curl + python) that measure p50/p95 token latency and embedding throughput.
- Redwood to track "time-to-first-token" metric during the quickstart and report it in the follow-up email.

Questions (auto-extracted):
- Can hosted support region pinning? (answered: yes, regional endpoints; dedicated for strict SLOs)
- Does Redwood provide SOC2 and SSO? (answered: yes)
